source.title: Fluctuations, Bias, Variance & Ensemble of Learners: Exact Asymptotics for Convex Losses in High-Dimension
source.authors: Bruno Loureiro; Cédric Gerbelot; Maria Refinetti; G. Sicuro; Florent Krzakala

record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes and plots double-descent test-error curves for random-feature learners, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own random-feature test-error curves and decompositions of test error into fluctuation-free and fluctuation terms. Values for the curves are shown in figures, not stated numerically. Cited results about double descent and triple descent are not recorded as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: The study derives exact asymptotic test-error curves, checked by simulation, for random-feature ridge and logistic regression as p/n varies. It shows an interpolation peak at p=n and splits test error into a fluctuation-free term and a fluctuation term. The fluctuation term, which ensembling removes, carries the peak. This bears on V4 (double descent in a non-deep model class) and on V6 (a variance-driven peak, plus an extra linear-peak bump). The method differs from the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors give a rigorous exact-asymptotic theory of fluctuations in ensembles of generalised linear models with convex losses. They show the double-descent peak comes from the fluctuation term tied to the random-feature weights, which ensembling suppresses. In the ridge case this rigorously confirms d'Ascoli et al. They also find that score averaging beats majority vote, with the two agreeing as K→∞, and that overparametrisation reduces disagreement between learners.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses high-dimensional asymptotic analysis and numerical experiments on random-feature generalized linear models, rather than the original deep-network size-sweep experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curves vary with ensemble size K, loss, estimator, and regularization setting; ridge and logistic results use different λ values.

fits_no_version.finding: The probability that two learners disagree (arccos(q1/q0)/π) decreases with overparametrisation and shows the interpolation kink (Fig. 5 center, Fig. 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overparametrisation increases agreement between independently initialised random-feature learners.

record.problems: The plotted curve values are not reported numerically in the text. Numerical results are finite experiments (50 or 10^3 runs, depending on figure), and no uncertainty intervals are reported. The paper notes that uniqueness of the general fixed-point solution is expected but leaves its proof for a longer version.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5's disagreement probability and confidence-score density are not test-error measures for the listed versions. Figure 4's covariance parameters are not test-error curves. Cited double-descent and triple-descent findings from other work are not results of this study. No epoch-wise or independent sample-size sweep is reported.

untested.parts: No deep networks are trained. Random features stand in only as a model of the lazy regime.
No sweep over epochs or training time.
Sample size n is never increased at fixed model size.
Only random-feature generalised linear models with erf features on synthetic Gaussian data are tested. Other model classes and real data are not.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location is tested.
Label-noise dependence is not tested (the targets are noiseless). Whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak is not tested: only λ=10^-4 and 10^-6 are used.
Complexity is not re-counted with an effective-parameter measure.

missing.what: An additional bump in the ridge fluctuation term δε_g at p/n=d/n (the 'linear peak'), separate from the divergence at p=n. It is evidence for multiple peaks.
A text statement that the K→∞ logistic test error is constant beyond the interpolation threshold.

record.verdict_notes: All curve values are figure-only, so peak heights for the logistic curves cannot be read from the text. r16 duplicates r3. The study does not vary regularization strength or label noise, so the V6 claims that the peak depends on noise and vanishes under optimal regularization remain untested.

versions.untested_parts: The study analyzes random-feature models, not deep networks, and does not test model-wise double descent in deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time is reported.
The study varies p/n at fixed n/d; it does not increase the number of training samples near the interpolation threshold while holding model size fixed.
Tests random-feature models with the reported losses and settings, not other model classes generally.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

The paper analyzes random-feature fluctuation contributions to the peak. It does not test label-noise dependence, triple or multiple descent as an original result, or whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates the peak.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective parameter measure to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: random features model (ridge regression), kernel limit
rows.operation_detail: Compared the kernel-limit test error with curves at finite p/n.
rows.note: The authors state that the kernel-limit error coincides with the fluctuation-free error for p>n.
rows.check: The kernel limit is the p→∞ limit and gives a single error level, not a curve over p/n, so it cannot show double descent. The paper only notes that it coincides with the fluctuation-free error for p>n.

relationships.condition: Random-feature ridge (λ=10^-6) and logistic (λ=10^-4) regression with finite ensemble size K, p/n varied at n/d=2
relationships.reason: Ridge test error diverges at p=n for every finite K and falls beyond it (r7–r12). The logistic curves show the interpolation feature for K=1–4 (r1–r4, figure-only).
relationships.display_finding: Ridge test error diverged at p=n and fell beyond it for every finite K, while logistic curves showed the interpolation feature for K=1–4.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Random-feature ridge (λ=10^-6) and logistic (λ=10^-4) regression with finite ensemble size K, p/n varied at n/d=2
source_check.reason: Figures 2 and 3 and Sections 2–3 identify double-descent behavior for finite ensembles and attribute its non-monotonic contribution to fluctuations.

relationships.reason: Averaging out the feature randomness leaves ridge error smooth with no peak (r13). Logistic error becomes constant beyond the threshold rather than falling again (r5). So the curve depends on the random-feature variance.
relationships.display_finding: Averaging away feature randomness left ridge error smooth without a peak and logistic error constant beyond the threshold.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Split the condition group: ridge has an explicitly absent interpolation peak (r13), warranting challenges; logistic retains an incomplete curve with constant error beyond the threshold (r5), warranting limits_scope.

relationships.condition: Random-feature ridge and logistic regression at near-zero regularization
relationships.reason: The fluctuation (variance) term δε_g carries the interpolation peak (r6, r15), and removing it by ensembling removes the peak (r5, r13). In ridge, δε_g also shows an extra linear-peak bump at p=d (r15).
relationships.display_finding: The fluctuation term δε_g carried the interpolation peak, which ensembling removed; ridge also showed an additional variance bump at p = d.
